Reading · the people who move back

1.1 Discuss. Would you rather live in a big city or a small town? Give two reasons, and one thing you would miss.

KEY WORDS

a returner somebody who goes back

anonymous not known to anybody

satisfaction how happy you are with something

to cope with to deal with something difficult

Why People Move Back

Every year a few thousand people leave the big cities for small towns, and the newspapers write about them warmly. Far fewer articles are written about the ones who come back, although there are a lot of them. In one survey of people who had moved out of British cities, about a third had returned within five years.

The reasons they give are rarely the reasons they expected. Very few people complain about the quiet, and almost nobody complains about the neighbours. What they complain about is transport. In a city you can rely on a bus arriving; in a small town you depend on a car, and if you do not have one, or cannot drive, the distance between you and everything else grows very quickly. One returner put it well: there was plenty of space and not enough ways to cross it.

Work is the second reason. There are simply more opportunities in a large city, and, more importantly, more different kinds of them. A small town may have enough jobs, but if you lose yours there may be very few others that match what you can do.

The third reason surprises people most. A lot of those who go back say they missed being anonymous. In a small town people care about you, which is warm when you want it and heavy when you do not.

None of this makes cities better. The same survey found that people who stayed in small towns reported higher satisfaction than city dwellers on almost every measure — less noise, more space, lower costs, and a stronger sense that they belonged somewhere. The point is narrower than that. A small town works well for people who have already succeeded in building a life that fits it, and badly for people who arrive expecting the town to build one for them.

If you are thinking of moving, the honest test is not whether you like the view. It is whether you would cope with it in February, on a Tuesday, with no car.

2

Grammar · quantifiers

PRESENTATION

A quantifier says how much or how many. The first thing to decide is whether the noun is countable or uncountable.

A Countable nouns only: many · a few · few · too many · fewer · There aren't many cinemas. We have a few parks.

B Uncountable nouns only: much · a little · little · too much · less · There isn't much noise. We have a little space.

C Both: a lot of · lots of · plenty of · some · any · no · enough · Plenty of things to do. Enough jobs.

D a few / a little = a small amount, and that is fine. few / little = almost none, and that is a problem. We have a few shops ✓ · We have few shops ✗ (a complaint).

Position of enough: before a noun — enough jobs · after an adjective or adverb — big enough · fast enough.

Countable (A)

Uncountable (B)

Both (C)

many restaurants

much traffic

a lot of people

a few friends

a little money

plenty of space

too many cars

too much noise

not enough buses

fewer shops than before

less crime than before

no cinema at all

ERROR WARNING

Don't drop some and any before plural and uncountable nouns — the commonest error in this lesson:

I'd like to ask you questions. ✗ → ask you some questions ✓ · We got there without trouble. ✗ → without any trouble ✓

Don't drop of: a lot bookshops ✗ → a lot of bookshops ✓ · plenty advice ✗ → plenty of advice ✓

Don't use plenty where you mean enough: I didn't bring plenty bags. ✗ → enough bags ✓

Word order: too much far ✗ → too far ✓ · enough fast ✗ → fast enough ✓ · Few of people know ✗ → Few people know ✓

In a positive statement, many sounds formal. We saw many butterflies → a lot of butterflies ✓ (many is normal in questions and negatives: How many? · not many)

3

Vocabulary · verbs and prepositions

PRESENTATION

Some verbs are always followed by the same preposition. The preposition is part of the word — learn them together.

A about · care about · complain about · worry about · think about · argue about (a topic)

B for · pay for · apologise for (a thing) · wait for · look for · ask for

C in · believe in · succeed in · take part in on · depend on · rely on · concentrate on

D to · belong to · listen to · apologise to (a person) · complain to (a person) with · argue with (a person) · cope with · agree with

Two verbs take two prepositions: apologise to somebody for something · complain to somebody about something.

PRONUNCIATION

Do not stress the preposition. The stress stays on the verb, and the preposition is weak: care about → /ˈkeər əbaʊt/ · rely on → /rɪˈlaɪ ɒn/ · belong to → /bɪˈlɒŋ tə/.

Stress patterns: Oo argue · worry · oO complain · believe · belong · depend · rely · succeed · oOoo apologise.

BEFORE YOU LISTEN

You will hear two friends disagreeing about whether small towns or big cities are better places to live. One of them grew up in a small town; the other has always been a city person.

WHY YOU DIDN'T HEAR IT

Quantifiers are almost never stressed, and the little word of inside them disappears completely. What survives is the noun after it, which is why you can hear cinemas clearly and miss a lot of entirely.

People rarely lose an argument out loud. Listen to the last thing the town person says: she accepts the facts and keeps her position anyway. In English that is done with but — there are definitely advantages, but I still miss my little home town. Notice where the stress falls.

Writing · describing the area where you live

WHAT YOUR DESCRIPTION HAS TO DO

You will write about the area you live in, for somebody who is thinking of moving there. It has three jobs:

Say what is there — with quantifiers, not just lists. Say what is missing — honestly. Say who it suits — and who it doesn't.

5.3 Turn each opinion into a claim with evidence. Use a quantifier.

HOW TO DO IT

A bare opinion is weak: The area is quiet.

A quantified claim is strong: The area is quiet — there are only two cafés and no bars at all.

1 The area is well connected. → There are four bus routes and the metro is ten minutes away.

2 It's not a good place for teenagers. →

3 It's cheaper than the centre. →

4 It's getting more crowded. →

ERROR WARNING

Three things go wrong in this kind of writing:

1 A list instead of a description. There is a park, a school, two shops and a mosque. — true, but it tells the reader nothing. Add a quantifier and a judgement: There are only two shops, which is enough for a weekday and not for a Sunday.

2 Many in a positive sentence. There are many cafés. → a lot of cafés ✓

3 Only good news. A description with no not enough and no too much is an advertisement, not a description — and the reader stops trusting it.

PLAN

Opening — where the area is and what kind of area it is, in one sentence.

What's there — three things, each with a quantifier and one concrete detail.

What's missing — one or two honest gaps, using not enough · too many · very little.

Closing — who it would suit, and who it would not.

5.5 Read the model. Then answer the questions below it.

MODEL

Yunusobod, if you have a car

I live in Yunusobod, on the northern edge of Tashkent, about twenty-five minutes from the centre by metro. There is plenty of green space — three proper parks within walking distance, and one of them is big enough to get lost in. There are a lot of small shops, most of them open until eleven, and a few good cafés, although not many stay open late. Rents are noticeably lower than in the centre.

What we do not have is enough for teenagers to do. There is no cinema at all, very little sport apart from football, and too many of the young people I know spend their evenings in the shopping centre because there is nowhere else. The traffic on the main road has also got much worse: people complain about it constantly and nobody in the district believes anything will change. It suits families with small children, and anyone who can rely on a car. It would not suit a nineteen-year-old.
